items.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 establishing sustainability reporting standards for voluntary use by undertakings protected by the value chain cap
items.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (Official Journal of the European Union)
items.locator: Article 2 and Article 4; recitals 3 and 5; Annex I, paragraphs 2, 6 to 8, 14, 18 and 24 to 43 (Basic Module, B1 to B11)
items.quote: This module is the target approach for micro-undertakings and constitutes a minimum requirement for other undertakings
items.why: The current text of the Basic Module and the source of the quotation. Eleven disclosures: B1 basis for preparation, B2 practices and policies, B3 energy and greenhouse gas emissions, B4 pollution, B5 biodiversity, B6 water, B7 resource use and waste, B8 workforce, B9 health and safety, B10 pay, collective bargaining and training, B11 convictions and fines for corruption and bribery. Several environmental items are marked voluntary for undertakings with 10 employees or less. Adopted 3 July 2026, published 21 September 2026, in force on the third day after publication. Official Journal text served by the Publications Office because EUR-Lex returned empty pages.

items.title: Commission Staff Working Document SWD(2026) 500 final, accompanying the two delegated regulations of 3 July 2026
items.locator: Section 4.3.2 'Quantified impacts of the VS', text and table, PDF page 21 (printed page 20); footnote 37
items.quote: followed by significantly lower recurring costs in the following years
items.why: Source of the figure. Estimated cost of applying the standard: Basic Module first year EUR 3,500 to 4,500 for undertakings with fewer than 20 employees and EUR 7,500 to 12,800 for those with 20 to 250; recurring EUR 2,000 to 2,300 and EUR 3,500 to 6,000. The estimates come from the cost-benefit analysis prepared for EFRAG on the 2024 standard and cover undertakings with up to 250 employees only; they are estimates for EU firms, in euros, not measured UK costs.

items.title: Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/1710 on a voluntary sustainability reporting standard for small and medium-sized undertakings
items.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (Official Journal of the European Union)
items.quote: It constitutes an intermediary solution to address market demand
items.why: The instrument the legacy briefing relied on. A non-binding recommendation that endorsed the EFRAG standard as a stopgap until a delegated act was adopted. Recital 5 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 says that from that regulation's entry into force the Recommendation should be considered as no longer producing any legal effects. Cite the regulation, not this, for the current text. Official Journal text served by the Publications Office.

items.title: Voluntary sustainability reporting standard for non-listed SMEs (VSME)
items.locator: Paragraphs 5, 22 to 44 (Basic Module, B1 to B11), in particular paragraphs 30, 31 and 42(b)
items.quote: The undertaking shall disclose its GHG intensity calculated by dividing
items.why: The original standard, delivered to the Commission on 17 December 2024, and the version most questionnaires and templates still follow. It differs from the 2026 regulation: this version asks for greenhouse gas intensity (paragraph 31) and a gender pay gap figure unless headcount is below 150 (paragraph 42(b)); the regulation drops the intensity line and asks for the pay gap only where the undertaking is already required by law to report it. A standard-setter's technical advice, not law.

items.title: Voluntary reporting standard for SMEs (VSME): concluded project page
items.locator: Opening paragraphs; 'VSME Digital Template and XBRL Taxonomy'
items.quote: On 17 December 2024, EFRAG delivered the VSME Standard along with the rest of the package to the European Commission.
items.why: Where the standard, its basis for conclusions, the cost-benefit analysis and the digital template are published. Caution: the page still says the standard 'will not be issued as a Delegated Act', which was overtaken by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560. No date is printed on the page.

items.title: Commission adopts revised sustainability reporting standards
items.publisher: European Commission, Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union
items.locator: News article, paragraphs on the voluntary reporting standard and on scrutiny
items.quote: The voluntary reporting standard provides a single, proportionate reference framework for sustainability reporting by smaller companies outside the scope of the CSRD.
items.why: The Commission's plain account of what the standard is for: answering requests from large companies and financial institutions. Written at adoption, when the act still faced two months of scrutiny by the European Parliament and the Council; it has since been published in the Official Journal.

items.title: Environmental reporting guidelines: including Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting requirements
items.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero; Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs; Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
items.locator: Landing page, 'Details'; guidance PDF (152 pages), chapter 2, page 29, and chapter 3 on voluntary reporting
items.quote: The government encourages all other companies to report similarly, although this remains voluntary.
items.why: The UK position for smaller firms: energy and carbon reporting is required of quoted companies and large companies and partnerships, and merely encouraged for everyone else. The guidance gives UK methods for energy and Scope 1 and 2 emissions that match what B3 asks for. Not updated since 2019: page 29 still prints size thresholds (£36 million, £18 million) that the Companies Act no longer uses.

items.title: 2026 post-implementation review of the SECR regulations 2018
items.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
items.locator: 'Objective 4: Proportionate reporting burden', pages 18 to 19, including Figure 3
items.quote: most businesses report good availability of core data
items.why: UK evidence that the core of the basic data set is obtainable: among companies already reporting, total energy use and Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions were mostly rated easy to compile. The respondents are large and quoted companies, not small firms, so this is indirect evidence for a smaller organisation.

items.title: UK government conversion factors for company reporting of greenhouse gas emissions
items.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
items.quote: The UK government conversion factors enable users to calculate and report greenhouse gas emissions from UK operations based on activity data.
items.why: The published factors that turn fuel and electricity use into Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions for UK operations, which is the arithmetic B3 requires. Updated each year; the 2026 set was published in June 2026. State in the method note which year's factors were used.

items.title: The Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (revised edition)
items.publisher: Greenhouse Gas Protocol (World Resources Institute and World Business Council for Sustainable Development)
items.locator: Chapter 4, 'Setting operational boundaries', printed page 25 (PDF page 27); chapter 5 on the base year, printed page 35 (PDF page 37)
items.quote: Companies shall separately account for and report on scopes 1 and 2 at a minimum.
items.why: The method behind the emissions line of the basic data set. It defines Scope 1 (sources the company owns or controls) and Scope 2 (purchased electricity) and requires a base year so that figures can be compared over time, which is what makes the data set refreshable. The existing list has the separate value-chain (Scope 3) standard under another criterion, not this one. A voluntary standard published by two non-governmental bodies; this is the revised edition dated March 2004, and later guidance from the same bodies was not read in this pass.

items.title: The Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013, regulation 12: Recording and record-keeping
items.quote: must be kept for at least three years from the date on which it was made
items.why: A binding UK rule under which part of the basic data set already exists. The responsible person must keep a record of reportable injuries, diseases and dangerous occurrences for at least three years, which is the raw material for the health and safety disclosure (B9: work-related accidents and fatalities). The legal definition of a reportable incident is not the same as the standard's 'recordable work-related accidents', so the two counts must be reconciled, not assumed equal. Great Britain; the page shows no outstanding changes.

items.title: The Equality Act 2010 (Gender Pay Gap Information) Regulations 2017, regulation 1: Citation, commencement, interpretation and application
items.locator: Regulation 1(2), definition of 'relevant employer'; regulation 2(1) for the six figures to be published
items.quote: an employer who has 250 or more employees on the snapshot date
items.why: Settles when the pay-gap line of the basic data set applies to a UK firm. The 2026 regulation asks for the gender pay gap only where the undertaking is already required by law to report it; in Great Britain that duty falls on private and voluntary sector employers with 250 or more employees on 5 April. Below that size the line can be left out. legislation.gov.uk carries this instrument only as originally made, so later amendments are not shown on the page; public authorities listed in Schedule 19 to the Equality Act 2010 are outside these regulations (regulation 1(6)).

items.title: Making environmental claims on goods and services (the Green Claims Code)
items.locator: Section 2, 'Business-to-business claims'; section 3, principles 'Claims must be truthful and accurate' and 'Claims must be substantiated'
items.quote: This guidance also applies (to a more limited extent) to businesses marketing to other businesses.
items.why: The rule that applies once the data set is published as a sales asset, which is what the top level of this criterion describes. Environmental statements made to win business must be truthful, clear and backed by evidence, and misleading advertising to other businesses is prohibited. A figure with no recorded method cannot be substantiated. Published 20 September 2021 and unchanged on the page read; it describes the law as it stood then (the Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008 and the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008) and was not checked in this pass against later changes to consumer law.

items.title: SMEs and Net Zero 2025: UK Net Zero Business Census report
items.locator: 'Tracking and measuring carbon emissions', page 17; summary table 'SME Net Zero Key Progress Indicators', page 16
items.quote: The proportion measuring their carbon footprint comfortably exceeds the proportion where this data has been requested by customers (20%)
items.why: A UK baseline for the emissions line. One in five smaller businesses measures a full or partial carbon footprint: 10% of those with no employees, 22% of micro, 30% of small and 51% of medium-sized businesses (table, page 16). So an assembled data set is still the exception. Based on 1,783 businesses in the 2025 UK Net Zero Business Census; publication date printed as October 2025. A survey report, not peer reviewed; self-reported; carbon only, with nothing on waste, workforce or conduct data.

items.title: Data Requests in Value Chains: The Effects of Corporate Sustainability Reporting on SMEs in The Netherlands
items.publisher: Niemann, Morssinkhof, van der Linden and de Vries, Sustainability 17(17), 8029 (MDPI); copy held in the Delft University of Technology repository
items.locator: Section 3.3, 'Perceived Relevance of ESG Data for SMEs Themselves' (article page 8, PDF page 9), with Figures 4 and 5
items.quote: More than half of the SMEs in the sample (52%) indicated that they consider this aspect relevant and that they actively collect data on it.
items.why: Peer-reviewed evidence on which parts of the basic data set small firms already hold. Health and safety data is the best kept (52%), which the authors link to existing safety law; only 21% both regard carbon emissions as relevant and collect the data, although carbon is the item customers ask for most. Tells a board where the gaps are likely to be. Survey of 431 Dutch firms in late 2024, 19% response rate; Dutch law and practice, not UK. Read in the university repository's copy of the final published version.

items.title: Engaging small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the low carbon agenda
items.publisher: Conway, Energy, Sustainability and Society 5, article 32 (Springer)
items.quote: Whilst the majority has taken steps to reduce their carbon impact, most do not monitor or set targets for managing carbon usage.
items.why: Peer-reviewed UK evidence for the gap between acting and measuring: small firms take practical steps but do not keep the numbers, which is the 'fragments' level of this criterion. Open access on the publisher's site. Limits: 141 respondents in one English county (Derbyshire), a questionnaire, published in 2015; use it for the pattern, not for a current rate. The British Business Bank survey gives the current UK figure.

items.title: Fostering convergence in SME sustainability reporting (OECD SME and Entrepreneurship Papers)
items.locator: Table 2.2, printed pages 18 to 19 (PDF pages 19 to 20); executive summary, printed page 6 (PDF page 7); Annex A, Table A A.1
items.quote: Most common indicators and metrics across SME frameworks
items.why: International comparator. The OECD compared the EU voluntary standard with other frameworks for small firms and lists the indicators they share: Scope 1 and 2 emissions, energy, water, waste, workforce characteristics, health and safety, and governance items. The overlap with B1 to B11 shows the basic data set is not an EU peculiarity, so a UK firm that assembles it is also equipped for non-EU askers. Approved 20 January 2025; describes the EU standard while still a draft, before Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 changed some datapoints.
